en: As for this *Śata-dharma-śāstra*, it is called a "gate" because it is the gateway for entering the Mahāyāna. Thus, one should know that this is the essential pivot of both the Nature (Xing) and Characteristics (Xiang) schools.
Among those who study the doctrines, there are none who can exhaustively master all dharma-gates without first clarifying these dharmas.
While the ancient supplementary notes merely take the text of the treatise itself as their commentary—thereby using the treatise to explain the treatise—is this not...?
Is this something that those with a beginner's mind can enter? It is because they do not know its origin.
Since there has been no commentary on the original treatise (*Mūla-śāstra*) from the past, it has simply been passed down as it was until now.

Although there are now commentaries on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the hundred dharmas are fully contained within the treatise itself, and the commentary merely follows the original text; thus, these hundred dharmas remain entirely unintelligible. This is due to the tradition of the lineage...

This is a general overview; thus, students simply do not know its essential points. Whenever the Old Man [Master Xuyun] instructed students, he always said that entering the Buddha-dharma must necessarily begin from this.
When the attendant Guangyi initially found it difficult, the Old Man taught him to investigate the original treatise (*śāstra*).
Consequently, Guangyi recorded the text of the treatise as a commentary, further incorporating the commentaries of three masters and synthesizing them to explain the treatise. This compilation...
Once these are unified, they become clear and easy to perceive. For this reason, this compilation is especially a preliminary step for entering into the *Śata-dharma-śāstra*.
Wherever the commentary (*ṭīkā*) was incomplete in its exposition of the meaning, I have drawn from the *Zhijie* (Direct Explanations) or the *Wen* (Questions), supplementing the meanings as follows.

Preface to the *Commentary on the Compendium of the Rules for the Mahāyāna Hundred Dharmas*, handwritten by the seventy-seven-year-old Elder Hanshan on a summer day in the Renxu year of the Tianqi era.
When the Great Master commented upon the sūtras and śāstras, he did not seek to display novelty nor flaunt the extraordinary; he proceeded directly from the fundamental intent of the original texts.

With a single glance, he saw through to the core; having first attained the meaning beyond words, he was able to harmonize and penetrate all things with such evenness, substantiality, and precision that he elucidated the texts and revealed their meanings, striving solely to capture the Buddha’s intent.

Thus, he not only revitalized the ancestral Way of the Middle Revival, but truly caused the sun of truth to shine brightly within the sky of his own nature. He was truly a great banner of light during this Dharma-ending age. Among his disciples of old...
Among those renowned as masters who have entered the inner sanctum and whose teacher-disciple relationship was one of perfect accord, there was Mr. Feng Xiaolian Qinan.
At that time, the Great Master had no leisure for the Way of the Dharma, yet it remained something still to be realized. Now, his writings are fully complete.
Yet our predecessors have already departed. How fortunate we are to have personally received instruction from the venerable masters of this age under their very seats;
how could we not each conceive the thought that they are beings of great dignity and difficult to encounter? At that time, Master Yizhong was the youngest in years yet the earliest in awakening;
scholars remarked that one must "scratch the eyes" [to acknowledge his progress] after three days. I, your unworthy servant, and the Master were parted beneath the Bodhi tree.
"It is just as it was yesterday. Yet your physical bearing and learning are entirely different from those of the man of old.

As for your diligent toil and profound research, you still say that such matters are merely a matter of forced effort. But when it comes to the moment of surrounding the assembly, your subtle words and profound meanings possess the air of a wild goose indifferent to humans;
they are like the mechanism of a hare leaping and a falcon swooping—whereas others are clumsy and stagnant."
The Master [Kuiji] resolved these points with the sharpness of a blade slicing through wood;

he grasped them in his mind and transmitted them through his speech, enabling those who heard him to feel their spirits leap with joy as if listening to the Perfect Sound (the Buddha’s voice) being proclaimed once more. There were those who could not fathom how this was so.
Alas! When the tiger roars, the wind grows fierce; when the dragon rises, the clouds gather. With the presence of Kuiji, the Way of Master Jñānaprabha flourished even further.
Regarding the Light: since its inception with [Hui]sheng and [Dao]zhao, the meaning of [Seng]tong’s longevity has become increasingly abundant.
Might Master Yi not be one who, mounting the wheel of his vows, continues the life of wisdom? Otherwise, how could his early awakening be such as this?

Following this, to enlarge through emptiness, to illuminate through humility, to substantiate through practice, and to reach fulfillment through realization—all these are the masterful deeds of the Master. This is the cultivation of the lineage.
What does this humble grass require from others? The *Baifaguiju Zuanzhu* (Annotations on the Hundred Rules) fully reveals the Master’s painstaking efforts;
yet, it merely discloses a small portion thereof. Since the Great Master has already provided a preface, I dare not add further words.

However, while the Master modestly wishes to keep this within his own treasury, I, your unworthy servant, desire that it be made public for the sake of all. Thus, I have ventured to compose these few words as an exhortation.

I am not quick-witted, and Heaven has cast my physical form aside; yet, I believe that within me there exists a noble form. Therefore, even while still a child, I harbored a transcendent aspiration.
When I heard that our Great Master’s Dharma-thunder had awakened the hibernating creatures, I leaped with joy and took refuge in him.

I have harbored this aspiration for many years. In the past, during the Gui-chou year, I accompanied my late father on an official tour to Hengzhou, where I happened to pay my respects to the Great Master at Linghu.
I was immediately accepted by him as a disciple. At that time, I observed that Master Xu-zhong-yi was exceptionally refined, alert, and quick-witted;
I knew he was a vessel for the Dharma, yet I did not yet know his ultimate direction. Then, in the summer of the Ding-si year, the Great Master retired to Mount Kuang-lu.
Beneath Mount Wuyuwu, having lost both my parents, I resolved to seek refuge there and pursue the path of world-transcendence.

In the spring of the Xin-you year, I finally entered the mountains with firm determination. The Great Master took pity on me; after I was admitted into his inner quarters, I was able to hear the essential points of the Dharma.
Day and night, I deliberated upon profound meanings with him until I gained a thorough penetration beyond words. I was filled with leaping joy—not only because...

This forgetting of form is, moreover, a forgetting of the mind. Without interruption even for eating or resting, one day he saw the *Bai fa gui ju zan shi* (Compendium and Explanation of the Hundred Rules and Standards) at the head of his desk.
He and Liu Xiaolian Zhongan opened the scroll together; after reading it once, he sighed three times, saying, "The Master’s refined meaning has entered the divine to such an extent!
Although my mind is not yet familiar with the cases of the school, I have long heard this discourse."

Even those who are veteran teachers and long-established scholars find it difficult to enter [this teaching]. This is because the commentaries on the treatises are concise in expression yet profound in meaning, and moreover, they are fragmentary and incomplete;

furthermore, as there were no ancient exegeses, many have been like those facing a blank wall. Recently, although there have been several schools of commentary on the root treatise, these have not yet been synthesized.
Even with respect to this, the situation remains the same; thus, I, a scholar of the final age, weep at the crossroads. Now, you—[the Master]...
In detailing this treatise, I have consulted various commentaries from both ancient and modern times beneath each name and definition, synthesizing them into a single coherent system.

Having personally received the heart-seal (citta-mudrā) of the Great Master, I have adjudicated among these sources; thus, the text is as easy to dissect as splitting firewood, and its meaning as clear as observing a flame.

Without the need for laborious searching or circuitous inquiry, he has thoroughly penetrated the source of the characteristics of dharmas; this is no different from the three carts holding pens [to record the teachings].
It has been several years since we last met; how is it that Master He’s awakening was so early and his entry into the Dharma so refined?

Is this not because those who extract the numinous roots from the empty soil are not easily found? Looking back, I and Master He share a great bond from our youth; I am ashamed that I have not [been able to assist him].
I am able to praise but a ten-thousandth part of it; I have briefly set this down to record the beginning and end of the Dharma’s conditions.

Postscript to the *Compilation and Explanation of the One Hundred Rules* (*Baifaguiju Zuan Shi*).
Since I first subdued my mind and cultivated pure karma, taking refuge in the Buddha Vehicle, I have harbored a resolve to transcend the mundane world.

I have deeply rejoiced in following the teachings to seek their source; yet, as the ocean of the Tathāgata’s Dharma is vast and boundless, and the sky of its meaning is expansive and profound, regarding the path of *śamatha*, I have not yet...
I was able to set my hand to it; yet every time I unrolled the scroll, I could not help but sigh at its boundless depth.

When I inquired of various venerable elders, they all instructed me that one must first clarify the *Awakening of Faith* and the treatises on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (the Hundred Dharmas), saying: "These are the pivotal keys to the entire Great Canon.
It is like a journey of ten thousand li: it begins with the feet. There has never been anyone who could reach such a destination without the steps of their feet having moved."
"Ten thousand *li*—this means that one must know the rules and measures of the hundred dharmas; these are but the steps beneath one's feet. Therefore it is said:

'If one clearly understands the hundred dharmas, one may enter the gate of the Mahāyāna. When I examined Lan'an’s supplementary commentary, I found its wording concise yet its meaning profound and obscure;
thus, I rarely grasped its essential points. In the autumn of the Bingyin year, Master Xugu of Kuangshan happened to come traveling to Huang..."

When Master Shanxi passed by Mount Baituo, I and my second elder brother met him at Wenshang. We first requested instruction on the Three Contemplations of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, followed by the *Awakening of Faith* and the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*.
Yet every word the Master uttered produced meanings that transcended conventional views; for every difficulty he addressed, his principles penetrated the profound and subtle.
This is what is meant by the lion’s roar, which is inherently distinct from that of the common beasts. One day, within the Master’s satchel...
In the midst [of my search], I obtained this compendium. My elder brother and I held it and read it three times over; before we knew it, our previous obstructions were suddenly cleared away.
The *Śata-dharmāḥ* (One Hundred Dharmas) is detailed and exhaustive, while the rules and regulations are concise and clear.

This will enable beginners to understand everything at a single glance, so that they no longer lament the sorrow of standing at a forked path. Holding this key, one may thoroughly explore the treasure trove and suddenly attain [enlightenment].
"A household treasure! How joyful this is! I said, "This is a rare Dharma; why not disseminate it throughout the world? The Master was modest and kept it secret.
I pressed him earnestly until he consented to have it carved into printing blocks, so as to broaden the gift of the Dharma.
May all students, through these words, attain the meaning and realize the mind through the definitive sense, so that they may not fail their teacher nor fail themselves. This is the preface.
Written and calligraphed by the disciple Hecatian Du, Xincheng Kaiyu,

The Commentary on the Gate of Illumination of the One Hundred Dharmas of the Mahāyāna, compiled and explained by Guangyi of Wuru on Mount Kuang.
Regarding the term "Mahā" (Great), its meaning is to distinguish it from the "Small" (Hīnayāna). This means that while the Small Vehicle consists of only seventy-five dharmas, the Mahāyāna...

Thus, there are one hundred dharmas. Regarding the term "vehicle" (*yāna*): it derives its name from the sense of "carrying" or "conveying. This is like the boats and carts of the world, which can transport heavy loads over long distances;
by analogy, the Bodhisattva mounts this Great Dharma to cross the river of birth and death, reach the land of Bodhi, and ascend the shore of Nirvāṇa.

While these names and meanings are mutually explained, it may also be said that the term is distinguished from the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) by taking "carrying" as its primary meaning. One hundred.
"Numbers" (*saṃkhyā*) refers to enumeration. "Dharmas" (*dharma*) refers to categories or models. This means there are ninety-four types of mundane dharmas and six types of supramundane dharmas;
thus, their total number is one hundred. Specifically, these are: eight mental factors (*citta-dharma*); fifty-one mental concomitants (*caitta-dharma*); eleven material factors (*rūpa-dharma*);
twenty-four factors dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra-dharma*); and [six] unconditioned factors (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Sixth: These constitute the hundred dharmas of the Mahāyāna. "Illumination" (*prajñā*) refers to the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) of a bodhisattva;

because it can shatter the darkness of ignorance (*avidyā*), it is called "wisdom-illumination. This distinguishes it from the tainted wisdom (*sāsrava-prajñā*) of ordinary beings, which cannot destroy the afflictions (*kleśa*).
"Gate" (*mukha*) signifies the sense of opening through without obstruction; that is to say, these hundred dharmas are common to both ordinary beings and sages.

By means of this gateway, it is further clarified that these one hundred dharmas constitute the very gateway for entering the Mahāyāna. As for "treatise" (*śāstra*), it refers to the definitive discernment of meaning;
that is, the selection of essential natures and characteristics, the instruction of later students, and the resolution of doubts—hence it is called a treatise.
Thus, the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, from among the six hundred and sixty dharmas within the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*,

extracted the essential framework and briefly recorded these one hundred dharma names and numbers to demonstrate them to later students, so that they might understand the great essentials of the myriad phenomena (*dharmas*).
All noble ones and ordinary beings, both mundane and supramundane, grasp these one hundred dharmas as being truly existent.
Because of this "self," one incurs the two kinds of birth and death: the *paricchinna* (segmented) and the *pariṇāma* (transformative).

If one can clearly and fully awaken to the fact that all things are devoid of self, then one transcends these two deaths; when the conceptualizations of both the noble and the ordinary are exhausted, this very state constitutes the gateway for entering the Mahāyāna.

Thus it is called the "Luminous Gateway of the One Hundred Dharmas of the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, the character "luminous" (*ming*) refers to the wisdom capable of contemplation, while the "one hundred dharmas" refers to...

The objects of contemplation—both this wisdom and these objects—are all gateways into the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, the purpose of the treatise is merely to definitively discern objects and wisdom with clarity and freedom from delusion.

Since the dharma-gate wherein both mind and objects are empty is by no means something that those of inferior faculties can receive, this principle-contemplation belongs entirely to the Mahāyāna; hence it is designated as "The Hundred [Verses] of the Mahāyāna."
The Gate of the Illumination of Dharma (*Dharmāloka-mukha*). This is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound.
It was composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu;
this is the name of the author of the treatise. The "One Hundred Dharmas" within the treatise were spoken by the Buddha and are contained within the Great Canon (*Tripiṭaka*).

This discourse encompasses all phenomena. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Bodhisattva Maitreya, out of compassion for sentient beings with wrong views who find it difficult to enter the True Dharma, descended from Tuṣita Heaven to the kingdom of Ayodhyā in Central India.
There, he expounded the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* for the Bodhisattva Asaṅga, systematically gathering all phenomena and condensing them into six hundred and sixty dharmas.

The principles of its nomenclature are nearly exhausted. The treatise consists of one hundred fascicles, which are roughly divided into five sections: first, the *Maulī Bhūmi* (Local Section); second, the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (Section on Compendium of Determinations);

third, the *Vijñāptimātrasaṃgrahaṇī* (Section on Compendium of Cognition-Only); fourth, the *Paryāyasaṃgrahaṇī* (Section on Compendium of Synonyms); and fifth, the *Vastusaṃgrahaṇī* (Section on Compendium of Entities).

Later, the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, seeing that the text was overly voluminous, abridged the enumeration of the names and numbers of the one hundred dharmas from within the *Maulī Bhūmi* of this treatise.
It causes the fundamental source of all phenomena to be grasped within one’s fingers and palms, much like dredging the nine rivers and channeling the myriad streams so they flow into the sea.
It is most concise and essential; in truth, it follows the teachings of the ancient sages and arranges them into systematic chapters.
Thus, it is also said to have established the lineage of Bodhisattvas, as detailed in separate transmissions, which I shall not record here at length.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang, by imperial decree. This is the name of the translator.

When Xuanzang first arrived in the Western Regions, he initially went to Nālandā Monastery, where he personally received instruction from the Master of Śāstra, Śīlabhadra, and studied the Dharma-gates of the *lakṣaṇa* school.
He uniquely inherited the transmission of the fundamental tenets of the *Vijñaptimātra* (Consciousness-Only) school, thereby subduing [opposing views].
His views were unique; he subdued the various non-Buddhist sects and his fame resounded throughout the Five Indies.

Therefore, he brought this treatise back to the Great Tang and, in accordance with an imperial edict from Emperor Taizong, translated it. "To translate" (*yi*) means to change; it refers to changing the Sanskrit language into the Chinese language, hence it is called "translation."
As the Blessed One said: "All phenomena (*dharma*) are without self.
Regarding the phrase "as the Blessed One said," this is originally spoken by the Buddha; it serves as the primary authority for the treatise, establishing the source from which the Dharma proceeds.
"All phenomena are without self" refers to the one hundred phenomena (*śata-dharma*) and the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*). Thus, the Blessed One taught the Dharma...
The "Master of all dharmas" refers to the Dharma that is taught. To say, however, that there is no self is to speak of the non-existence of what is spoken.
Why is this? Because the Buddha fundamentally has no dharma to speak, nor does he bestow any real dharma upon others;
he merely strikes down and shatters the attachments of sentient beings as appropriate to their circumstances. Furthermore, "all dharmas" refers to the world...

This is the dharma of all noble and ordinary beings, both mundane and supramundane. Ordinary people falsely cling to the five aggregates—the body and mind—and this provisional self as being the "self.

Non-Buddhists falsely cling to a soul (*ātman*) and so forth as being the "self. Followers of the Lesser Vehicle falsely cling to their partial views regarding the *nirvāṇa* they grasp as being the "self.
Bodhisattvas falsely perceive that there are sentient beings to be saved and Buddhas to be sought. This is not [the true nature].
I cannot. Regarding the *tathatā* (suchness) realized, there is both realization and attainment, yet the notion of "self" has not been forgotten.
Thus, whether they be worldly ordinary people or non-Buddhists, or those of the three vehicles who have transcended the world, all possess the grasping at a self.
Therefore, the Buddha refutes this with a single word, "Non-": he says, "All phenomena are without self," meaning that all phenomena are originally without self.
Therefore, we know that those who speak of "all dharmas" are referring to the dharmas clung to by sentient beings; these are not what the Buddha taught.
Because sentient beings falsely cling to them as existing, the Buddha merely says they are non-existent. How could there be any dharma?
This single word "non-existence" is itself a tool used out of necessity to shatter their attachments. Furthermore, how could there be any real dharma?
O people! Alas! This is the guiding principle of our Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma and the fundamental source of all phenomena.

Therefore, this treatise sets forth its thesis for the sake of humanity, intending to say: one should act as the World-Honored One has taught—namely, that one must understand that all dharmas are without self.
If a student truly realizes selflessness, then more than half the work of the Mahāyāna Dharma-gate will have been accomplished.
"What are all phenomena? In what sense are they selfless?
These questions are posed with the intention that people may achieve awakening and realize that all phenomena are fundamentally and originally selfless.
There are five kinds of questions. First is the question for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings.

This refers to a bodhisattva who, knowing that all things are selfless while sentient beings do not, asks the Buddha out of a desire to bring them benefit and happiness, so that they may attain realization, transform from the mundane to the sacred, and become sages.
Second is the question of lack of understanding. This refers to asking because one does not clearly comprehend the phenomena and principles of all matters.

Regarding questions directed at others: third, the question of ignorance, which refers to asking others while being darkened by folly and deluded regarding the distinction between principle and phenomena;
fourth, the question of testing, which refers to asking another about what one already knows in order to verify whether the other person knows it or not;
fifth, the question of insolent provocation, which refers to asking others in a playful or mocking manner out of arrogance and improper conduct.
This bodhisattva has posed this one question, which is, among the five questions, the inquiry concerning the benefit and happiness of sentient beings.
Should there be two questions, I shall first explain the initial one.
Regarding "all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*), there are briefly five kinds: first, mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*); second, mental concomitants (*caitta-dharma*); third, ...
1) Form-dharmas; 2) Mind-dharmas; 3) Mental-associative dharmas; 4) Mind-dissociative formative dharmas;
and 5) Unconditioned dharmas. This enumeration of the numbers and listing of the names is intended to resolve doubts.
Since the previous question did not know what constitutes "all dharmas," nor what constitutes "selflessness," this answer states that, speaking generally, by means of these [categories]...
Sentient beings give rise to immeasurable passions, and the dharmas that accord with their capacities are likewise immeasurable;
these are expounded as the Tripiṭaka, comprising nine divisions in total. Now, to summarize their essential principles, there are briefly five types.

Among these five, the first four respond to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), while the last one concerns supramundane unconditioned phenomena (*lokottara-asaṃskṛta-dharma*). Furthermore, regarding these five dharmas, if...

There are only four [stages]: those who see only the first are called ordinary worldlings and externalists; those who see only the last are called adherents of the Lesser Vehicle with its partial emptiness.
If one perceives the unconditioned within the conditioned, thereby transcending the mundane world while remaining within it, such a person is called a Mahāyāna Bodhisattva.
First, because it is supreme; second, because it is associated with this; third, because it is a manifested reflection; fourth, because of the distinctions in its stages;
fifth, because it is that which is revealed. Such is the sequence.
This explains the reason for the sequence of the preceding enumeration of dharmas. First, as for listing the mental factors (*caitta*) at the head:

because all phenomena of the three realms, whether superior or inferior, are produced by this single mind alone; and because all causes and effects—whether pertaining to the noble ones or ordinary beings, or being defiled or pure—are established in dependence upon the mind.
Since this [mind] is the most preeminent, it is listed first. Second, as for those associated with it: these are the aforementioned mental factors.
This applies to all phenomena (*dharma*). However, the sovereign mind (*citta-rāja*) is fundamentally neither good nor evil; it cannot act alone, for it must rely on its attendants to possess power.
These attendants must harmonize with the sovereign; only then can there be internal and external correspondence, making it capable of accomplishing its tasks.
Therefore, all phenomena belonging to the mind are the mind’s servants; they correspond with the mind, and only then [can they function].
Because they are capable of producing karma, they are listed next. Third, as for the "reflected images that appear," these are precisely the aforementioned dharmas of form (*rūpa*).

This means that these dharmas of form do not originally come from the outside; rather, they are the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the eight consciousnesses, which are reflections of one's own mind.
The eight consciousnesses are like a mirror, and these dharmas of form are like the images within the mirror. Form does not become form of itself; it arises through the transformation of the mind.

Manifestation (*pratibhāsa*). Since the eight consciousnesses are collectively designated as the "transformer" (*pariṇāma*) and the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) is the "transformed," it is necessary to clarify that the essence of form is ultimately mind-only;

thus, it is called a "reflected image" (*pratibimba*) and is listed as the third [category]. Regarding the differentiation of the four divisions (*caturbhāga*), these are precisely the previously mentioned mental factors dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*).
Although these belong to the domain of the mind, they do not associate with the mind; they comprise the first three [categories] in total.

These are merely distinctions of states (*avasthā*) within the dharmas that are falsely conceptualized; therefore, they follow immediately after [the preceding section]. These four aforementioned stages are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).

The intent of composing this treatise is precisely to demonstrate the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) by means of these very conditioned phenomena, because that which is to be demonstrated is fundamentally unconditioned. Thus, it concludes with this. Therefore, it says "like... [referring to the simile].
This is the sequence.

Regarding the first category, mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*), there are briefly eight kinds: (1) visual consciousness, (2) auditory consciousness, (3) olfactory consciousness, (4) gustatory consciousness, (5) tactile consciousness, and (6) mental consciousness.

This list enumerates the names of the first six consciousnesses; all are established based on their respective supporting faculties (*indriya*). They possess five meanings: support (*āśraya*), production (*utpāda*), belonging (*parigraha*), assistance (*sahakārin*), and similarity (*sārūpya*). Regarding these:
with the exception of the faculty that produces the consciousness, the other four are *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinatives) compounds, meaning "the consciousness that depends upon the faculty.

The consciousness produced by the faculty is a *bahuvrīhi* (possessive determinative) compound, meaning "that which has the faculty as its basis. As the Sūtra says: "Originally depending on a single brilliant essence, it was divided..."
The formation of the six harmonious aggregates (*ṣaḍ-samavasarga*) and their clarity and vigor constitute the substance of the eight consciousnesses. Fundamentally, there is only the true mind;
through delusion, it becomes the eight consciousnesses. Now, as they discern objects through the six gates, they receive six designations.
When reflecting upon the eye, that which is able to differentiate forms is called the "eye-consciousness," and so forth. It is like a single object stored within a single room.

It is like a monkey. In the six sense bases, there is someone who responds whenever called; thus, they are distinct from one another. Furthermore, the first five consciousnesses derive their names from the five faculties.
They possess only the function of illumination. At the very first moment of perceiving an object, there is fundamentally no discrimination.

However, that which involves discrimination in the second moment belongs to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Thus, the first five [consciousnesses] rely upon the five forms [of the faculties].
The consciousness of the [first] five faculties is the sixth, which is the consciousness produced by the mind (*manas*), because the seventh mind serves as the faculty for those six.

A supplementary note states: "Although all six groups of consciousness function in dependence upon the mind, this [designation] follows the specific (non-common) mental consciousness and is termed 'dependent' or 'produced' and so forth;
thus, there is no confusion with the five groups of sensory consciousness. Alternatively, it is called "mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*) because it depends solely upon the mind.

"Identifying by name. The mind (*manas*) is not analogous [to the other five]. The supplementary commentary states: "This distinguishes how the six consciousnesses receive their names based on their respective sense organs (*indriya*). Question:
Since the bodies of the first six consciousnesses all arise in dependence upon the mind (*manas*), they should all be called "mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*).

Why is it that only the sixth is given the specific name "mental consciousness"? Furthermore, the teachings speak of the transformation of the mind, the intellect, and the mental consciousness; this clarifies— [...the distinction between them.]

[Objection: Since it is known that the preceding six [consciousnesses] are all designated by the same name, "mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*), does the present mention of "mental consciousness" not result in a confusion with the [other] five, as they share the same name?

[Treatise] Response: Although all six groups of consciousness (*ṣaḍ-vijñānakāya*) arise in dependence upon the mind (*manas*), this [sixth consciousness] alone is named according to its specific faculty (*indriya*).
Just as the first five consciousnesses each have their respective supporting faculties (*indriya*), this sixth consciousness does not share these with the preceding five;

rather, it relies solely upon the mind (*manas*) as its faculty, and is thus designated "mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*), being the consciousness of the mind, just like the group of the five consciousnesses.

Based on the faculties of form and so forth, because it relies solely upon the mind (*manas*), it is called "consciousness of the mind" (*mano-vijñāna*); this is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound.

Here, it is precisely by virtue of its function as discernment (*vijñapti*) that it receives its name. One must not insist that the first six [consciousnesses] collectively constitute the single characteristic of the mind, lest there be confusion.
These names are established based on their respective supporting faculties (indriya); therefore, they do not overlap.

If one were to say that the first six consciousnesses all function by depending on the mental faculty (manas), then the sixth would overlap with the first five and become one with them. Now, however, we are distinguishing the specific faculties upon which each depends;
while the sixth depends solely on the mental faculty as its support, it is thus called "mental consciousness" (mano-vijñāna). How could this possibly overlap with the preceding five?

That is to say, while their transformation is common [to all], their reliance upon the sense faculties (*indriya*) is not. This refers to the designation "discerning" (*vijñapti*) based on reliance upon the sense faculties.
The scriptural teaching that "mind, thought, and consciousness transform" has a distinct meaning. Therefore, it concludes: "Mind and thought are not analogous [to consciousness]."
The seventh is the *manas-vijñāna*.
This seventh consciousness is designated by its associated [mental factors]. In full, it should be called *kliṣṭa-manas*, which translates as "defiled mind.
This means that because it is constantly accompanied by the four afflictions—greed, hatred, views, and pride—it is termed "defiled."
It is defiled. That which constantly and critically deliberates is called "manas" (mind). Constantly and critically examining and deliberating, it conceives of the eighth consciousness as the self.

Such deliberation exists only in the seventh [consciousness] and is absent in the other consciousnesses; therefore, it alone is given the name "manas. Furthermore, that which is capable of discerning objects is called "vijñāna" (consciousness).
Question: Previously, the sixth was named "mano-vijñāna" (mental consciousness); now, this consciousness is also so named. What is the distinction?
Question: What is meant by this? Answer: The sixth consciousness derives its name from its reliance on a sense organ; this consciousness establishes its designation based on its own essential nature.
Although the sixth consciousness can discriminate between the good and bad qualities of the five sensory objects, it is through this consciousness that they are transmitted, continued, and grasped.
Regarding "based on the faculty" (*indriya*): the faculty is the seventh consciousness. Its essential nature is precisely the nature of discrimination.
As for the eighth *ālaya-vijñāna*, this eighth consciousness receives its name based on its functional capacity; because it possesses the threefold meaning of "storehouse," it is called *ālaya*.

*Ālaya*. In terms of its true meaning (*tattva*), it is translated as "non-perishing" (*amukta*). Because *tathatā* (suchness) flows through the transitions of birth and death without being lost or destroyed, it is called "non-perishing.
Master Xuanzang translates it according to its functional meaning as the "storehouse consciousness" (*ālayavijñāna*), because it is able to contain and store the seeds of all phenomena.
This "storehouse" has three meanings: that which stores, that which is stored, and the grasping at self-love (*ātmasneha*). Because...

It is able to contain and store the seeds of both good and evil, remaining indestructible throughout kalpas; from the perspective of its function as a repository for these seeds, it is called "the capable store" (ālaya).
Furthermore, this consciousness is the locus where the seeds of the preceding sense-faculties, the body, and the environmental world—whether wholesome or unwholesome—are stored;
from the perspective of its function as that which receives perfuming, it is called "the stored" (ālaya). Moreover, this store-consciousness is firmly grasped by the manas as being the self.
Because it is the internal self, it is called "the storehouse cherished through self-love. By virtue of these three meanings, it receives the name "ālaya" (storehouse).

"Ālaya" is precisely consciousness (*vijñāna*); this is a *karmadhāraya* compound. Therefore, it is said that its function is given as its designation. The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states: "The ālayavijñāna is the Tathāgatagarbha.
This consciousness is the name for *tathatā* (suchness) while still entangled in defilements; it is the Buddha-nature of sentient beings and the [source] of the myriad dharmas.
The Root and Source: The fundamental origin of good and evil, and the dwelling place for both the holy and the ordinary.

Because all phenomena of the mundane and supramundane realms—whether defiled or pure—are manifested through the transformations of this consciousness, it is said that "the myriad dharmas are but consciousness.

This refers to the above-mentioned eight consciousnesses, which, though differing in name, are identical in essence; they are collectively termed the "Mind-King" (*cittarāja*). Following these are the fifty-one mental factors (*caitta*).

All dharmas are the messengers of the King of Mind; they merely differ in their respective quantities. Therefore, Master Xuanzang composed the *Verses on the Eight Consciousnesses* (*Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-kārikā*) to provide a standard for them.
Second, as for the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), there are briefly fifty-one kinds, divided into six categories. First, the universal factors (*sarvatraga*)... [have] five.
Five: (1) There are five object-specific mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviśeṣa*); (2) eleven wholesome factors (*kuśala*); (3) six afflictions (*kleśa*);
(4) twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*); and (5) four indeterminate factors (*aniyata*).
This is an enumeration of the states of the fifty-one mental factors (*caitta*). As for "mental factors," they are those phenomena that belong to the mind.
They always arise in dependence upon the mind, are associated with the mind, and are bound to the mind; possessing these three characteristics, they are called mental factors.

Therefore, they are called "mental concomitants" (*caitta*). Just as objects belonging to oneself receive the designation "mine," these mental concomitants arise in accordance with wholesome or unwholesome objects, giving rise to aversion, attachment, and so forth; because they assist in accomplishing the activities of the mind, they receive the name "mental concomitants.

Since all arising thoughts and mental movements do not transcend the two paths of the wholesome and the unwholesome, there are merely the distinctions of the six categories. As for those that are omnipresent (*sarvatraga*):
Since the mind itself is non-existent, the thoughts that arise are produced by the internal perfuming of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

As for the "object-specific" mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviśeṣa*), they arise because each separately takes its own object as a condition. These two categories alone do not fall outside the range of the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Among them, there are only eleven wholesome mental factors, whereas the unwholesome mental factors consist of the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*).
Sixth: the twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). Here, wholesome habits are few while unwholesome habits are many;
thus it is fitting that virtuous people are few, while those who are not virtuous are many. As for the four indeterminate factors (*aniyata*), they possess both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
This concludes the general enumeration of names and categories; hereafter follows their detailed explanation in successive order.
The five universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*) are: attention (*manas*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*).

This explains the meaning of the names for the primary mental factors (*caitta-dharma*). Regarding the term "universal" (*sarva*): it means all-pervasive, signifying that there is no state to which they do not reach.
"Universal factors" (*sarvatraga*) refers to the mental activities—that is, the mind capable of cognition—wherein their objects are the mind itself.
They function as the objects of focus for that [mind]. These five mental factors are "universal" because they exist in four ways:
namely, they pervade all virtuous and non-virtuous natures; they pervade all three realms and nine stages; they pervade all durations of time, both long and short;
and they pervade all consciousnesses, arising simultaneously with the eight types of consciousness regardless of what the primary mind may be. However—

Because it arises as soon as [the mind] exists, it receives this name. That is to say, all those within the category of sentient beings who have not yet been able to leave behind discursive thought possess this.

Although these are listed as five names, they collectively constitute a single mind. It is because these five factors are fully present that the consciousness which apprehends an object is only established in a single moment of thought.
Hereafter, first the root treatise (*mūla-śāstra*) is cited, followed by the new commentary (*vṛtti*).

To explain this: where the meaning is insufficient, it is supplemented. Regarding the supplementation of the meaning: the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* takes mental attention (*manasikāra*) as primary, while the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* takes contact (*sparśa*) as primary.

This is because, according to the *Yogācāra*, the contemplative practices (*vipaśyanā*) of those in the Two Vehicles and the provisional teaching Bodhisattvas are all cultivated based on mental attention;

this applies universally to both ordinary beings and sages. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* takes contact as primary, proceeding directly from the threefold conjunction [of sense organ, object, and consciousness].
The arising of contact takes the object as its precursor; this is explained solely in terms of consciousness and pertains only to ordinary beings.
These differences have never been distinguished until now.
First, regarding *manasikāra* (attention): its nature (essence) is the ability to alert the mind; its function (activity) is to draw the mind toward its object.
That is to say, this alerting [process] causes the seeds of the mind that are to arise to be drawn toward and directed toward the object; therefore, it is called attention (*manasikāra*).
Mental attention (*manasikāra*) refers to the initial stage of the arising of the mind and the movement of thought.

Its essence and function consist in alerting the mind to cause it to arise and leading the mind toward its object. There are two meanings to this "alerting": first, causing the mind that has not yet arisen to arise;
second, causing the mind that has already arisen to lead itself toward the object. Question: Does mental attention alert the mind while it is in the state of a seed, or...

Manifestation. Answer: It exists in the state of a seed. Because its intrinsic nature is clear and sharp, even while in the state of a seed, if an object arrives and is able to alert the mind, it causes manifestation to arise. This is illustrated by the analogy of many people staying together in one room;
when an outsider comes as a thief, one person among them who is naturally light-sleeping is able to awaken the others. This person, of his own...
Although the body has never yet arisen, it is able to awaken others and cause them to arise.

The seeds of mental attention (*manasikāra*) can both awaken those various mental seeds to produce manifest activity (*pravṛtti*), and can also cause the manifest activity of the mind to move toward its objects of perception (*ālambana*).

The former is the essential nature (*svabhāva*); the latter is the functional activity (*karma*). Supplementary explanation: This refers to the essence of the eight consciousnesses, which is like a profound and still abyss, originally...

There is no *manas* (mentation). Due to the internal perfuming and activation of seeds, there arises *manaskāra* (attention); at this stage, good and evil have not yet been distinguished, as there is merely the movement of thought.
Therefore, it does not induce the mental factors (*caitta*).

Regarding the second, contact (*sparśa*): its intrinsic nature is the differentiation of the transformation resulting from the conjunction of the three [factors], which causes the mind and mental factors to touch their objects;
its function is to serve as the basis for feeling, perception, volition, and so forth.

Supplementary Explanation: Regarding the statement that "contact (*sparśa*) refers to the differentiation of the transformation resulting from the conjunction of the three," this indicates that contact possesses a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
it is substantial and not merely nominal. The term "conjunction of the three" refers to the sense faculty (*indriya*), the object (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

The term "differentiation" means that at the moment of the conjunction of the three, mental factors (*caitta*) have not yet arisen; because they have conjoined but have not yet grasped [the object], it still belongs to what resembles direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and it remains...
Because it is the fundamental locus, the present contact is precisely the thought that grasps an object.

As soon as there is even a slight grasping and attachment, the tranquil essence becomes turbid and agitated, and thus the mental factors (*caitta*) of liking and disliking arise; hence, it is called "discrimination" (*vikalpa*).

This means that this single thought of grasping also possesses a function similar to the preceding three [mental factors] in producing the mind; therefore, the treatise explains "discrimination" by way of similarity. Transformation...
"Alteration" means that through grasping, the preceding three [aggregates] undergo alteration and lose their essential nature; this constitutes inference (*anumāna*).
Regarding the statement that "mind and mental factors have contact with objects as their nature," this refers to the function of contact;

it means that mind and mental factors rely entirely upon the power of contact to be able to draw themselves toward and contact objects. It is the basis for feeling, perception, volition, and so forth.

Regarding "that which acts": although the mind contacts objects and objects in turn contact the mind, the union of mind and object gives rise to wholesome and unwholesome habitual energies (*vāsanā*).

These are about to give birth to mental factors (*caitta*), yet they remain contained within it without having yet manifested; therefore, it is said to be the basis for sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), and so forth.
As the Sūtra says: "The self-mind grasps the self-mind; that which is not illusion becomes illusory phenomena. If one does not grasp, there is nothing that is not [illusory]."
Illusion. This is an emphatic statement that grasping at even a single dharma causes immense affliction. Therefore, this treatise discusses the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness;
yet, even when these three coincide in one place, wholesome or unwholesome actions cannot arise without contact (*sparśa*). Thus, contact possesses a real essence and function.
The meaning of this contact (*sparśa*) is most subtle; it cannot be elucidated without grasping the individual characters.

Regarding the three feelings (*vedanā*): their nature is the experiencing of objects that are disagreeable, agreeable, or neither; their function is to give rise to craving (*tṛṣṇā*), because they can produce the desires for union, separation, or neither.
"Feeling" (vedanā) means experiencing. "Experiencing" consists of receiving and containing. If one experiences an adverse object, a mind arises that desires to separate from it;
if one experiences a favorable object, a mind arises that desires to unite with it;
if one experiences an object that is neither adverse nor favorable, a state of equanimity arises, wherein one neither desires to unite nor desires to separate. This is the nature of feeling.
Furthermore, because it serves as the basis for craving (*tṛṣṇā*), it is able to give rise to affection; this is its function of enjoyment.
Fourth, perception (*saṃjñā*) has the nature of grasping the characteristics (*nimitta*) of objects, and its activity is the establishment of various names and expressions (*nāma-pada*).
That is to say, one must first establish the specific boundaries and characteristics of an object before being able to subsequently give rise to various names and expressions.

Regarding "perception" (*saṃjñā*): it refers to that which, tossed and driven by the winds of objects, establishes its own objective domain and employs names and conventions; this constitutes its essence and function.
"Establishing" means the sense of grasping an image. That is to say, this mental perception first establishes boundaries within objects such as forms and sounds and thereby grasps their images.
Because of grasping these images, one subsequently gives rise to names and conventions, such as "this is form," "this is sound," and so forth.
The five types of volition (*cetanā*) have the nature of causing the mind to act; their function is to employ the mind toward virtuous categories and so forth.

That is to say, they are able to apprehend the characteristics of the true causes and other factors regarding objects, and by driving and employing one's own mind, they cause it to perform virtuous and other such actions.
Volition (*cetanā*) has as its essential nature the ability to deliberate upon correct causes and erroneous causes, weighing what is feasible and what is not.
Its functional activity consists of driving and employing one’s own mind to perform good or evil deeds, and to bring about what is right or wrong. Question:
What is the difference between attention (*manasikāra*) and volition? Answer: Attention is like the movement of a horse; volition is like the rider. The horse merely proceeds straight ahead.
One cannot avoid the dangerous and seek the level by oneself; it is through the rider that one causes [the horse] to avoid the former and seek the latter.
Mental reflection (*manasikāra*) is likewise: it prevents the mind from wandering at will, causing it instead to abandon the deviant and resort to the correct.

Therefore it is said: "I desire to know your origin, O Desire: you are born from mental reflection (*saṃkalpa*). If I do not mentally reflect upon you, then you shall not arise. Furthermore, it is said: "There is no reflection..."
[The Master] said: "Be cautious in your thinking. He also said: "Deliberate three times before acting. [Supplementary Explanation:

From the stage of *manasikāra* (attention) to that of *cetanā* (volition), once the thoughts of good or evil have already formed, it is absolutely impossible to stop them. Therefore, the subsequent category of object-specific mental factors (*viṣayaviśeṣālambana*) constitutes the state of mind that necessarily acts upon those intentions.

The second category consists of the five object-specific mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviṣaya-ka-caitta*), namely: desire (*chanda*), resolve (*adhimokṣa*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).

They are called "object-specific" because the objects perceived by these five mental factors are each distinct; they do not, like the universal factors (*sarvatraga*), perceive a single common object.
This is because they arise by perceiving their respective objects individually. They are designated by the names of their four specific objects.

These are the object-specific mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviṣaya*). That is to say: desire (*chanda*) has the object that is desired; resolve (*adhimokṣa*) has the object that is determined; mindfulness (*smṛti*) has the object previously experienced;

concentration (*samādhi*) has the object of observation; and wisdom (*prajñā*) has the nature of discerning those four objects. Therefore, they are not the same as the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*).
*Supplementary Note:* These five mental factors are necessarily present in every state of mind. This applies equally to wholesome and unwholesome states. They are cultivated...
The same applies to application (*prayoga*).
First, desire (*chanda*): its essential nature is the aspiration for an object of interest, and its function is to serve as the basis for diligence (*vīrya*).
As for desire, its essence consists in the longing and expectation for an object of interest; it takes diligence as its support. This is...
As for its function: it is the longing for certain union with desired objects and the longing for certain separation from undesired objects.
That is to say, one desires life for what is loved and desires death for what is hated; thus, both delight and aversion are termed "desire" (*chanda*).
Therefore, among all worldly and world-transcending dharmas, there is none that is not accomplished through aspiration.
Thus, by aspiring to worldly dharmas, one accomplishes worldly fruits; by aspiring to world-transcending dharmas, one accomplishes world-transcending fruits.
How vital it is that one’s aspirations must not be improper! When the ancients set fixed periods to seek realization of unsurpassed bodhi, it was their aspiration that drove them.
[This refers to] power (*bala*). [Supplementary Note: The Buddha taught that sentient beings have various types of desires, not only regarding *bodhi*. The same applies to the following four.
Second, resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) has the nature of maintaining a determined object and the function of being unshakeable. That is to say:
Through the power of reasoning and scriptural authority regarding the correct and the erroneous, one examines and definitively ascertains the object of apprehension;

because it cannot be diverted by other conditions, there is no resolute conviction whatsoever regarding an object of doubt. Furthermore, that which is not a mind of definitive examination likewise lacks resolute conviction.
For this reason, resolute conviction is not included among the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*).
Resolve (*adhimokṣa*) refers to the certain knowledge regarding an object that it can be acted upon, such that one cannot be led astray.

To say "decisively sealing and maintaining so as to be unleadable" means that by relying on the power of evidence—whether from false teachings or correct teachings, or from fallacious reasoning or valid reasoning—one thoroughly examines and clearly decides upon the object of apprehension, thereby sealing and firmly maintaining it. It is because of this that [it differs].

Because conditions cannot pull it away or seize it, it is called "resolute conviction" (*adhimokṣa*). As it is said: "Form is like a mass of foam; feeling is like a bubble on the water; perception is like a mirage;
mental formations are like the trunk of a plantain tree; consciousness is like a magical illusion. Thus, being decisively superior, it cannot be led astray. As the saying goes:
"The commander of the three armies may be captured, but the will of a commoner cannot be taken away. An ancient master said:

"Let them take 'neither mind nor Buddha' as they will; I myself am 'mind itself is Buddha. If one is half-doubting and half-believing, or if one is as if present and yet as if absent, this is called the state of hesitation (*vicikitsā*).

There is absolutely no resolute understanding (*adhimukti*) here. Even if one maintains the conviction, if there is no heart of decisive judgment that cuts through like a single stroke of a blade, there is likewise no resolute understanding.
For this reason, resolute understanding is not included among the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*)."
Furthermore, this nature of desire (*chanda*) subsumes the three natures—wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral—as will be explained later in the section on laziness (*kausīdya*).

Regarding the three types of mindfulness (*smṛti*): their nature is to cause the mind to clearly remember and not forget objects previously experienced; their function is to serve as the basis for meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This means that by repeatedly recollecting and maintaining objects previously perceived, one prevents them from being lost, thereby being able to induce concentration.
"Mindfulness" (*smṛti*) refers to causing the mind to clearly apprehend and not forget its object of engagement.
"That which has been previously practiced" refers to matters that have been habitually cultivated. "Taking clear mindfulness as the basis for concentration" means being alert and free from delusion.

It is vivid and distinct; keep this in mind and let it remain present without a moment’s lapse. By practicing in this manner, distracted thoughts will naturally settle, which is called right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).
As the ancients said: "A single thought lasts ten thousand years; ten thousand years are but a single thought"—this is precisely what that means.

The four concentrations (*samādhi*) have the nature of causing the mind to focus intently on the object of observation without distraction; their function is to serve as the basis for wisdom (*jñāna*).

That is to say, within the objects of observation—whether they be those characterized by gain, loss, or neither—the concentration causes the mind to focus intently without distraction. Based upon this, there arises a definitive wisdom.
The phrase "mind focused intently" indicates that one is able to abide wherever one wishes to abide; it does not refer exclusively to a single object.
"Concentration" (samādhi) refers to focusing the mind one-pointedly upon the object of observation.

As for the "object of observation," it refers to the five aggregates (pañca-skandha), impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and so forth. To focus the mind without distraction is the function based upon concentration.
Regarding the function of daily application within ordinary circumstances: one applies the mind to observe, asking, "What is form? What is sensation? Form is... [etc.]
"What is it that receives [the object]? and so forth. By focusing the mind in this way with single-minded concentration and without distraction, there will naturally be a point of entry.
Through this, the original luminosity reveals itself and the wisdom of decisive discernment arises. As for the phrase "the mind focuses," this indicates what object this mind intends to take;
it means one can cause the mind to abide in that very object, rather than referring to a single object alone.
[End of commentary]. Supplemental Explanation: This interpretation relies solely on meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) and does not encompass worldly phenomena (*laukika-dharma*).
For instance, [the stories of] "pouring water over a tile" and "catching cicadas with a stick" are both matters of meditative power; why should it apply exclusively to Chan meditation?
The five types of wisdom have the nature of discerning the objects of observation and the function of severing doubt;
that is to say, when observing objects that are either beneficial, detrimental, or neither, one attains certainty through the investigation and inquiry of wisdom.
"Wisdom" (prajñā) refers to being clearly aware and free from doubt regarding the objects of one's activity.
"Discerning and severing doubt" means that within the context of the gains and losses of all phenomena, one employs the mind of wisdom to investigate and differentiate;
only thereafter does the mind reach a state of certainty, free from uncertainty. This wisdom arises from meditative concentration—what is called "wisdom born of concentration. Both good and evil...
Thus, concentration and wisdom are like the two wheels of a chariot or the two wings of a bird; neither can be lacking.

Wisdom must necessarily arise from concentration, and through this, one attains decisiveness. Therefore, it is said that when the mind is unmoving in single-mindedness, one is called "entering the various dhyānas."
To realize that objects are non-arising is called *prajñā* (wisdom). [Supplementary Note: Mundane intelligence and eloquence are also termed "clever wisdom.

Regarding the three wholesome [roots] and the eleven [factors]: these are: first, faith; second, diligence; third, shame (*hrī*); fourth, dread of blame (*apatrāpya*); fifth, non-attachment; sixth, non-hatred;
seventh, non-delusion; eighth, pliancy (*praśrabdhi*); ninth, heedfulness (*apramāda*); tenth, equanimity (*upekṣā*); and eleventh, non-harming (*avihiṃsā*).
This is the enumeration of the names of the wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*). The following treatise explains their characteristics. First, faith (*śraddhā*):

its nature is a profound acceptance, delight, and aspiration toward reality, virtue, and capability, with mental purity as its essence; its function is to counteract lack of faith and to take pleasure in the wholesome.
Briefly, there are three types of distinctions in faith: first, faith in real existence (*astitva-śraddhā*), which refers to [faith] regarding the reality of all phenomena.

1. Because of deep faith and acceptance regarding phenomena and principles; 2. because of faith in the possession of virtues, meaning because of deep faith and delight in the true and pure virtues of the Three Jewels;
3. because of faith in the possession of capability, meaning because of deep faith that all mundane and supramundane virtues have the power to be attained and brought forth through aspiration.
By means of this, one counteracts lack of faith, and that mind comes to love and delight in the cultivation and realization of the mundane and supramundane.

"Worldly goodness" refers to patience (*kṣānti*), which is to say, resolute conviction (*adhimukti*); this is the cause of faith. "Delightful desire" refers to aspiration (*chanda*), which is the fruit of faith.

To state precisely what the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of this faith is: is it not already stated that its nature is the purity of mind? This faith is transparent and capable of purifying the mind and other factors;
because the mind is preeminent, it is designated by the name "purity of mind. It is like a water-clearing jewel (*vimalaprabha-maṇi*) that can clarify turbid water. Furthermore, all...
Regarding the defiled dharmas, each has its own specific characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Among them, lack of faith (*āśraddhya*) alone has the nature of turbidity;

it not only possesses this turbid self-characteristic itself, but can also cause other minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) to become turbid, just as an extremely filthy object soils both itself and others. Faith is the direct opposite of that; therefore, clarity is its characteristic.
The following explains the eleven mental factors associated with faith (*śraddhā*). Regarding "faith": it refers to sincerity and trust, free from doubt.

First, "believing in actual existence" means that regarding all the actual facts and principles of the mundane and supramundane taught by the Buddhas—namely, the true causes and true fruits—one is able to have deep faith and accept them within the mind, rather than being led astray by erroneous matters or principles.
It is that which is set in motion by false causes and false effects; this is the cause of faith. Second, faith in those possessing virtue:

this refers to having deep faith and a fond inclination toward the virtues of the Three Jewels—the Dharma-body, prajñā, and liberation—which are truly pure, and not being deluded or confused by the three qualities (guṇas) of the Sāṃkhya school or the fourteen qualities of the Vaiśeṣika school. Third, faith in those possessing capability.
This refers to having deep faith in all conditioned wholesome states (*sāsrava-kuśala*) and unconditioned wholesome states (*anāsrava-kuśala*).
Whoever exerts effort in this regard will be able to attain the fruit and accomplish the work of the Path. Thus, one gives rise to a sense of rare wonder and seeks to surely attain these two;
this is faith in the fruit. By the power of this faith, one counteracts lack of faith and takes delight in the cultivation and realization of both worldly and world-transcending states.
It takes worldly goodness as its functional activity. Therefore it is said: "Faith is the source of the Path and the mother of merit;

faith can surely lead one to the stage of the Tathāgata. Question: Profound patience and the aspiration for [the Dharma] constitute faith in cause and effect. What, then, is the intrinsic nature of faith?
Answer: Did I not say previously that its nature is the purity of the mind? However, the intrinsic nature of faith is clear and limpid;

it is capable of purifying defiled minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*). Because the mind is preeminent, it is designated by the name "purity of mind," as this does not apply to the mental factors.
It is like the water-clearing jewel: if it enters the water one inch, the water becomes clear for one inch; if it enters the water one foot, the water becomes clear for one foot. Therefore...
It is said: "If a clear pearl is cast into turbid water, the turbid water cannot fail to become clear; if pure faith is cast into a defiled mind, the defiled mind cannot fail to become pure.
Supplemental Explanation: Faith is like the water-clearing pearl, and a person’s distracted mind is like turbid water.
If one beholds a Buddha image and gives rise to a single thought of faith and reverence, the mind immediately becomes pure.
Regarding the second, diligence (*vīrya*): its nature is valorous exertion toward the tasks of cultivating the wholesome and abandoning the unwholesome;

its function is to counteract laziness and bring wholesome qualities to fulfillment. "Valor" (*vīra*) indicates that diligence excludes all defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*), while "exertion" (*utsāha*) indicates it excludes the pure neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
This demonstrates that diligence is comprised exclusively within the category of the wholesome (*kuśala*).
Regarding "diligence" (*vīrya*): it refers to being courageous in reforming evil and transforming toward the good. As for the matters of cultivating the good and abandoning the evil:
this means causing unarisen good to arise, causing arisen good to expand, suppressing unarisen evil so that it does not arise, and severing arisen evil so that it does not continue.
Regarding the statement that "courage" signifies superior progress: it means that in every thought-moment one advances toward higher excellence and increasing development.
This is "retrogression. If one practices defiled dharmas, even if they increase, it is called retrogression in relation to all wholesome qualities, for it cannot be called progress.

Regarding the expression "resisting to manifest purity": just as when washing a soiled garment, the primary aim is to make it clean and white, so too, in severing evil, the primary aim is pure goodness.
Therefore, this purity belongs to wholesome dharmas; it is purified through the application of effort.

Because it is not of the nature of the non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), and because of these two meanings, this diligence is shown to be comprised within the category of the wholesome (*kuśala*).

Third, shame (*hrī*) has as its nature the honoring and respecting of the noble and the good based on the power of oneself and the Dharma; it counteracts lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and brings about the cessation of evil.

It is the action of conduct (*caryā-karma*). This refers to the sense of self-respect regarding one's own qualities, which serves as the antidote to shamelessness (*anapatrāpya*) by feeling shame for one’s faults and evils, thereby bringing all unwholesome behaviors to rest.
As for the term "shame" (*hrī*), it means to feel ashamed; that is, it arises based on respect for oneself and, furthermore, for others.
The Dharma arises as a source of great esteem and superior influence. One reflects:

"I possess this majestic and dignified body of seven feet, and I am fully endowed with the luminous and spiritual Buddha-nature. To fail to perform virtuous deeds and instead commit various evils—is this not shameful?
By virtue of these two kinds of superior power, whenever one encounters any person who is noble, virtuous, or possessed of merit...
All people will give rise to respect and conceive a sense of profound esteem for them, treating them as a father and serving them as a teacher.
Furthermore, they will feel shame regarding their own faults and must reform them; they will feel shame regarding their own evils and must reform them.
Thus, they are able to counteract the lack of shame and refrain from all unwholesome deeds.

The fourth is *apatrāpya* (moral dread). Its nature is to reject violence and evil by relying on the power of the world; its function is to counteract *anapatrāpya* (lack of moral dread) and to bring about the cessation of unwholesome conduct.

That is to say, by relying on the predominant influence of worldly censure and aversion, one rejects violence and evil, feels shame for transgressions and faults, counteracts *anapatrāpya*, and brings all unwholesome karma to rest.
Regarding "shame" (*hrī*): it is the mind that feels self-reproach. This means that, based on the predominance of worldly censure and the predominance of others' aversion, one reflects:
"If such a person performs such an act, it is censurable and loathsome; since I am now a person who is thus detested and loathed by others, am I not ashamed?
It is through the power of these two predominant factors that one perceives [one's own] violence.
One who is rebellious is treated with lightness and kept at a distance; one who commits evil is rejected and not befriended.

Furthermore, by feeling shame for one’s former ignorance and being humiliated by the transgressions and evils once committed, one is thus able to apply the antidote against shamelessness and bring all unwholesome conduct to rest.

The fifth, non-attachment (*alobha*), has the nature of being unattached toward existence and the requisites for existence; its function is to counteract attachment and to act as a basis for the wholesome.
These three factors, beginning with non-attachment, are called "roots" because their efficacy in producing the wholesome is supreme.
Just as when grasses and trees possess roots, they subsequently produce trunks, stems, branches, and leaves, so too do these [roots] proximately [produce the wholesome].

Because it serves as the antidote to the three unwholesome roots: "existence" refers to the fruit of the three realms of existence; "the equipment for existence" refers to the causes of the three realms of existence.
As for "non-attachment," it means being weary of and detached from the causes and fruits of the three realms, lacking any craving or clinging.
Its essential nature is to serve as the antidote to craving and clinging, and its function is to act as the wholesome.
Sixth, non-hatred (*adveṣa*) has the nature of being without resentment toward suffering and the instruments of suffering. Its function is to counteract hatred and to perform wholesome deeds.

When a wholesome mind arises, regardless of the object it encounters, it is characterized by neither attachment nor resentment toward existence and so forth; it is established through the contemplation of existence and so forth.

They do not necessarily depend on those [objects]. As with the previously mentioned *hrī* (moral shame) and *apatrāpya* (moral dread), these two are established by observing the wholesome and the unwholesome;

therefore, both of these two types pervade all wholesome minds. Regarding "non-hatred" (*adveṣa*): its essential nature is the non-arising of hatred toward the fruits of suffering within the three realms and the causes of suffering within the three realms.
Its function is to serve as the direct antidote to hatred and to perform wholesome deeds. Question: This non-greed and non-hatred...
Regarding the two roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), their objects of focus (*ālambana*) differ; therefore, they should not coexist and do not pervade all wholesome minds. Answer:

When a wholesome mind arises, whatever object it encounters, it simply regards that object as the basis for existence (*bhava*) and the instruments of existence (*bhavopakarana*), or as suffering (*duḥkha*) and the instruments of suffering (*duḥkhopakarana*).

It merely remains without attachment (*rāga*) or aversion (*dveṣa*) toward the object. Because this mind observes existence and so forth, or suffering and so forth, these two [roots] are established based on the observing mind.
The names [of these two dharmas] do not mean that they take existence, suffering, and so forth as their objects.

Just as the two dharmas of shame (*hrī*) and dread-of-blame (*apatrāpya*) were previously established with two names based on observing the wholesome and the unwholesome, yet they do not take those wholesome and unwholesome states as their objects,
so too these two dharmas both pervade all wholesome minds.

Seventh, non-delusion (*amoha*) has the nature of clear understanding regarding all phenomena and principles. Its function is to counteract delusion and to perform wholesome deeds. What is called "delusion" is none other than ignorance (*avidyā*).
Since it now clearly understands and comprehends all phenomena and principles, it is termed "non-delusion. Thus, clear understanding is taken as the essence of non-delusion.
As for "all phenomena and principles," briefly they are the Four Noble Truths; extensively, they are the Twelve [Links of Dependent Origination].
Because one applies effort directed toward that object, one is able to understand it clearly; its function is to counteract ignorance and perform wholesome deeds.
Eighth, pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) means being free from heaviness and rigidity; its nature is the fitness of body and mind through their being well-regulated and harmonized; it counteracts torpor.

Its function is to settle and transform the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). This means that it suppresses and eliminates those factors that obstruct meditative concentration (*samādhi*), thereby causing the basis upon which one relies to become transformed into a state of ease and well-being.

Regarding the term "pliancy" (*praśrabdhi*): it refers to the coarseness (*dausthulya*) of greed and delusion, which causes the body and mind to be dull and heavy; now, by distancing oneself from this coarseness...
It is "light" because it counteracts heavy torpor; it is "ease" because it renders the body and mind pliant, harmonious, and joyful; its nature is to enable the practitioner to undertake tasks;
its remedial function is to counteract torpor; and its activity is the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). To explain this further:
these methods for subduing and eliminating the obstacle of torpor which hinders meditative concentration cause the coarse and heavy body and mind that serve as the basis to be transformed.
Because it transforms [the mind] into pliancy and ease.
Ninth, non-negligence (*apramāda*) consists of diligence and the three roots. Its nature is to guard and cultivate that which is to be abandoned and cultivated.

Its function is to counteract negligence and to bring to completion all mundane and supramundane wholesome deeds. That is to say, these four factors [diligence and the three roots] operate with respect to abandonment and cultivation.
The ability to prevent and cultivate all matters is called non-heedlessness (*apramāda*). It does not possess a separate substantial entity, as it lacks any distinct characteristic;
for within the prevention of evil matters and the cultivation of wholesome matters, it has no function apart from the four primary faculties.
Regarding "heedfulness" (*apramāda*): it is the functional capacity for prevention and cultivation based upon diligence and the three roots.
That is to say, it prevents the arising of the evils to be abandoned and induces the increase of the wholesome matters to be cultivated; thus it is called "functional capacity.
This very prevention and cultivation constitutes its essential nature (*svabhāva*). It serves as the antidote to heedlessness and brings all things to complete fulfillment.
Wholesome activities constitute its functional operation. The *Yanyi* (Exegesis) states: "Diligence and wisdom guard the mind so that it does not transgress against sensory objects;
this is called non-laxity (*apramāda*). It further states: "The root of non-laxity is deep and firm, difficult to uproot.
Because of non-laxity, all roots of goodness attain growth. Next, it explains that this non-laxity has no separate essential nature; it is simply diligence (*vīrya*).
The three faculties are able to both prevent evil and cultivate goodness within all matters;

this specific functional capacity for prevention and cultivation is what is called "heedfulness" (*apramāda*). It is not a separate entity existing apart from these four dharmas, because it has no distinct basis other than those four.
Equanimity in the ten stages of practice has the nature of causing the mind to be even, upright, and to abide without effort through the three roots of diligence.
Its function is to counteract restlessness and to bring about peaceful abiding; that is, these four factors cause the mind to remain far removed from obstacles such as restlessness.

Tranquil abiding is called equanimity (*upekṣā*). It is an even, upright, and effortless state of dwelling. The distinctions of equanimity are differentiated according to its initial, middle, and final stages.
Through heedfulness (*apramāda*), one first eliminates defilements; equanimity then causes the mind to abide in tranquility. This [equanimity] has no separate substantial entity.
Just as with heedfulness, because there is no function of signlessness apart from those four dharmas, that which can bring about tranquility is precisely those four dharmas;
and that which is brought to tranquility is precisely the mind and so forth.
Regarding "equanimity of speech and action," this refers to the three roots of diligence (*vīrya*).
It enables one's own mind to become balanced and upright, abiding naturally and spontaneously without relying on effort; this constitutes its essence.
